claims.statement: Poland had approximately 11,762 publicly accessible charging points at the end of 2025, 36% more than a year earlier, including about 4,400 DC points.

The live EIPA registry listed 701 registered entities on 2026-08-24 and exposes legal names, CPO and/or mobility-provider identifiers, city, country, website, and registration date; this is a concrete top-of-funnel list, not a count of 701 addressable 20-500-connector fleets.
Registered EIPA readers can download separate JSON files for operators, charging pools, stations, points, and dynamic data, with operator contact fields and identifiers linking the asset hierarchy.

EIPA's documented dynamic record contains price, a binary operational-availability field, a free-or-busy field, and timestamps; access requires registration and is rate-limited, and UDT disclaims responsibility for the timeliness of operator-provided registry data.

AFIR Article 20 requires public-point operator/owner contact and identifiers plus operational status, availability, and ad-hoc price to be available through free, unrestricted APIs and national access points.

Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/655 requires static changes to be reflected within 24 hours, dynamic changes within one minute, source-side quality controls, and DATEX II formatting from 14 April 2026; it also requires Member States to monitor and address persistent data-quality problems.

The AFIR/EIPA layer can support fleet mapping and outage-led prospecting, but public out-of-order signals do not establish a separate reliability-operations budget or prove who has authority to buy outside an existing CPO, backend, installer, or OEM contract.

The public feed is not a diagnostic feed: its documented state fields cannot identify whether a failed charging attempt came from grid power, physical damage, safety protection, cellular connectivity, the backend, RFID, payment or authorization, vehicle handshake, power electronics, or connector locking.

Open Charge Alliance says the CPO is best positioned to attribute failures because successful charging depends on the station, CSMS, mobility/payment partners, app or card, and vehicle; OCPP alone is a message protocol and is not responsible for uptime.

When the station remains online and the service operator has authorized CSMS access, OCPP 1.6 and 2.0.1 provide useful remote actions including reset, connector unlock, status trigger, logs/diagnostics, firmware update, availability change, and configuration or variable reads/writes.

It is unknown what share of Polish mixed-brand fleets can grant a third party concurrent or replacement CSMS access, remote-command permission, diagnostic logs, payment evidence, and firmware rights without breaching backend, cybersecurity, warranty, or finance contracts.

ABB reports that customers on its own connected-services platform have 60% of service cases solved remotely, but that OEM-specific figure does not establish a cross-brand remote-close rate for an independent desk.

ABB bundles 24/7/365 monitoring, remote updates, troubleshooting, defined remote and on-site response stages, spare-parts coordination, and warranty service, and says repairs are exclusively performed by ABB-certified personnel or customer-selected personnel trained and certified by ABB.

A peer-reviewed field test of 655 US public DC fast-charging ports found 73.3% functional and observed screen/error, payment, initiation, network, and connector failures; its result conflicted with providers' reported 95-98% uptime. This demonstrates a measurement gap but is not Polish fault-frequency evidence.

GreenWay already markets in Poland an end-to-end business offer covering deployment, continuous monitoring, user management, settlement, servicing, reporting, and 24/7 operational support from single sites to large fleets.

Warsaw-based EVia Charge already markets essentially the proposed vendor-neutral offer: OCPP 1.6/2.0 multi-brand integration, connector-level monitoring, automatic fault detection, billing, 24/7 technical support, on-site support, and individually quoted SLAs.

A transparent European software benchmark is inexpensive relative to a managed service: E-Flux lists EUR 5.50 per AC socket/month and EUR 10.40 per DC socket/month and includes issue alerts plus remote reset and connector unlock.

Polish charging stations are subject to UDT technical examination before operation and after repair or modernization, with documentation review, inspection, and possible functional or load tests; UDT states a complete application is handled within 30 days.
No reviewed source establishes a recurring Polish budget for an independent reliability desk that is separate from CPMS, CPO-management, installer, warranty, or OEM service contracts.

EIPA identifies the responsible legal operator but does not identify the internal economic buyer; depending on ownership and contracts, authority could sit with a CPO operations lead, property/facilities owner, fleet manager, procurement, installer, financier, or OEM service owner.

No authoritative evidence found quantifies Polish technician density, travel radius and call-out cost, spare-parts lead time, after-hours burden, mixed-brand first-time-fix rate, or UDT-driven return-to-service delay for the target fleet segment.

A founder with at most five hours per day can plausibly run a business-hours 30-50-connector pilot, but cannot personally promise the 24/7 monitoring and response already marketed by direct competitors; scaling requires paid on-call coverage and field capacity before it creates software-like economics.

A research pricing case of PLN 120 per connector/month with a PLN 6,000 account minimum could produce a planning gross margin of roughly 35-45% only if field labor, travel, parts, and UDT costs are passed through and human incident time remains low; no source validates that price or workload.

Under the founder snapshot definition and without double-counting distributions, a conditional path to PLN 5 million of founder net worth requires about 4,700 connectors at PLN 120/month, 25% EBITDA, a debt-free 3.5x EBITDA value, and 85% founder ownership; that is about 40% of Poland's entire 2025 public-point base and therefore requires major market growth, CEE expansion, or incumbent displacement that current evidence does not support.

AFIR provides free and unrestricted access to the specified public data, but commercial storage, enrichment, cold-outreach use of EIPA contact data, and reuse of non-public OCPP, session, warranty, and repair records still require documented contractual and privacy rights.

The mixed-brand remote-close rate and the combined remote-or-one-visit-close rate remain unknown; ABB's 60% remote figure is not transferable, and neither public status data nor OCPP documentation supplies a Polish denominator.

contrary_evidence: EVia Charge already advertises a vendor-neutral OCPP 1.6/2.0 platform with 24/7 monitoring, billing, fault detection, technical support, and on-site service in Warsaw.
GreenWay sells continuous monitoring, settlement, service, reporting, and 24/7 operations as one established CEE bundle.
ABB can bundle monitoring, remote updates, certified repair, field response, warranty, and parts and reports 60% remote resolution on its connected platform.
E-Flux prices alerts and remote reset/unlock at only EUR 5.50 per AC socket/month and EUR 10.40 per DC socket/month, compressing the software-only value.
EIPA status fields are too shallow to assign fault ownership, and UDT disclaims timeliness of operator-provided data.
Public reliability evidence shows failures but does not prove Polish willingness to pay an additional independent operator.
The operational moat depends on certified technicians, parts, travel, on-call coverage, and regulated return-to-service work rather than scalable software alone.

economics.acquisition_route: Register for the EIPA reader files, join operator-to-pool-to-station-to-point records, and segment legal operators with an estimated 20-500 connectors. Use public websites to identify the CPO operations lead, head of e-mobility, facilities/fleet owner, or procurement role. Send a connector-level status-quality report only as an invitation to a contract-gap review, not as a claimed diagnosis. The first sale must disclose the current CPMS, OEM, warranty, maintenance, and installer responsibility matrix before any pilot quote.
economics.capital_required_pln: PLN 30,000-60,000 for a no-inventory business-hours pilot: CPMS and integration, security review, insurance/legal contracts, data pipeline, limited travel, and subcontractor deposits. A credible 24/7 NOC, national technician commitments, or owned spare-parts stock would likely exceed the founder-compatible pilot scope and is not included.
economics.founder_net_worth_path: {"definition_used": "Founder-owned business equity plus accumulated personal cash and distributions minus liabilities, excluding the primary residence. Retained earnings are reflected only through business value and are not double-counted; this path counts no founder distributions while corporate employment continues and assumes 95-100% of distributable cash is reinvested.", "milestones": ["Months 0-3: one prepaid 50-connector pilot at PLN 6,000 MRR with production access and contract exclusions documented; no founder net-worth value assigned.", "End of year 2: 500 connectors at PLN 120/month equals PLN 720,000 ARR; reach positive contribution economics and near break-even after paid operating coverage, with optional distributions held to 0-5% and otherwise reinvested.", "End of year 4: 2,000 connectors equals PLN 2.88 million ARR; at 15-20% EBITDA this is PLN 432,000-576,000 EBITDA. It therefore requires substantial market growth, CEE expansion, or displacement of established CPO/OEM bundles, plus a service business valued at 3.5x EBITDA despite field intensity and customer concentration. Treat this as the minimum scale hurdle, not a forecast."}
economics.founder_time: At most 3-5 hours/day for a 30-50-connector business-hours pilot, with no personal 24/7 promise. Founder handles data, reports, integrations, and scheduled escalation; a contracted duty operator is required before any after-hours SLA. At roughly 100-200 connectors, hire or contract a full-time operations lead unless measured incident minutes per connector are exceptionally low. This remains unverified and incidents can conflict with the founder's employment hours.
economics.gross_margin_basis: At 100 connectors, revenue would be PLN 12,000/month. At an explicit planning FX assumption of PLN 4.30/EUR, the E-Flux software benchmark implies PLN 2,365-4,472/month; add an inferred PLN 2,500-4,000 for human triage, ticketing, reporting, security/telecom allocation, and business-hours on-call capacity. That leaves PLN 3,528-7,135, or 29-59%, before CAC, service credits, bad debt, and any non-pass-through field cost. Use only 35-45% as a planning gross margin until ticket data prove otherwise; 24/7 coverage or high incident time can erase it.
economics.payback: For a 50-connector account at the PLN 6,000 minimum and a 40% planning gross margin, monthly gross profit is about PLN 2,400. Cap founder-led cash CAC plus onboarding at PLN 12,000 to target five-month gross-profit payback. No source validates the conversion rate, sales cycle, CAC, or onboarding effort, so this is a stop/go threshold rather than a forecast.
economics.pricing: Research estimate, not buyer evidence: PLN 120 per connector per month with a PLN 6,000 monthly account minimum for business-hours monitoring, remote triage, ticket ownership, and monthly evidence reporting; PLN 350 per dispatched incident for coordination; technician labor, travel, parts, OEM escalation, UDT fees, and service credits remain separately quoted or passed through. The software-only benchmark is EUR 5.50 per AC socket/month and EUR 10.40 per DC socket/month from E-Flux.
economics.retention_or_repeat: Proposed 90-day prepaid pilot followed by a 12-month contract, with renewal tied to agreed connector-level availability, mean time to acknowledge, remote-close rate, repeat-fault rate, and first-visit-close rate. Target monthly gross logo churn below 1.5%, but retention is unproven and can be broken by OEM warranty changes, backend migration, charger replacement, or bundling by the incumbent CPO.

fingerprint.compounding_advantage: Vendor-specific remote-remedy playbooks, reliable backend integrations, regional dispatch coverage, parts staging, and measured first-response and first-time-fix performance compound together. Route and technician density improve margins beyond what monitoring software alone can deliver.
fingerprint.customer: Regional charge-point operators and retail, hotel, parking, fleet, or municipal site owners operating 20-500 mixed-brand public chargers in Poland and nearby CEE markets.
fingerprint.distribution_mechanism: Continuously analyze the mandatory public operational-status feeds to identify fleets with recurring visible outages, send the responsible owner a quantified diagnostic sample, and convert to a paid monitored pilot. Separately, let charger installers embed the desk in every handover so they can sell an SLA without building a round-the-clock operations team.
fingerprint.offer_and_business_model: Connect to OCPP/backend feeds and required public status data, attempt safe remote remedies, classify faults, maintain payment and API evidence, and dispatch the correct qualified technician with parts context. Start as a managed network-operations service and automate the common faults; do not pretend that adding software later automatically removes field-service constraints.
fingerprint.payer_and_paid_event: The fleet owner pays a recurring fee per connector for monitoring, remote triage, data-quality compliance, and ticket management, plus a pre-agreed coordination fee for each field repair; payment recurs monthly against a transparent service report.
fingerprint.problem_trigger: A charger reports out-of-order, repeated payment or session failures breach a site SLA, AFIR data are stale, or a property owner cannot determine whether the fault belongs to connectivity, backend, payment, power, or hardware.

founder_fit: Strong analytical fit with data ingestion, anomaly detection, OCPP event analysis, automation, and the founder's renewable-installation adjacency.

A business-hours 30-50-connector paid pilot can fit the founder's five-hour daily limit and PLN 100,000 capital envelope if software is rented and field work, travel, parts, and UDT costs are passed through.

The market-standard promise is 24/7 monitoring and support; the founder cannot personally deliver that while employed and would need an on-call partner or hire before roughly 100-200 connectors or any hard after-hours SLA.
The operational moat is precisely the least founder-compatible layer: certified technicians, parts, travel density, warranty coordination, and incident response rather than AI or software alone.
risks: No separate budget: buyers may treat monitoring and uptime as already included in CPO, CPMS, installer, warranty, or OEM contracts.
No control rights: the desk may see an outage but be unable to issue safe remote commands, access logs, change firmware, or authorize repair.
Measurement liability: a binary public status can disagree with actual charge success, creating false accusations and poor prospecting.
Warranty and cybersecurity liability from third-party access or intervention.
Direct substitution by GreenWay, EVia, OEM service, and low-cost multi-brand CPMS products.
24/7 customer expectation conflicts with part-time founder availability and forces early fixed operating cost.
Field coordination scales with incidents, geography, parts, and people; software does not remove those constraints.
UDT and certified-repair requirements can delay return to service and create documentation obligations.
Customer concentration is likely because each fleet sale carries many connectors, weakening private-company valuation.
The founder-wealth target requires thousands of connectors and expansion or displacement before any route to PLN 5 million becomes credible.
thesis: An independent desk could create value for 20-500-connector mixed-brand fleets only where the asset owner has an explicit gap in existing CPMS, CPO, installer, warranty, and OEM contracts and can delegate production CSMS access plus service coordination. AFIR and EIPA provide a concrete fleet and outage-prospecting layer, but not diagnostic telemetry, buying authority, or evidence of a separate budget. Current evidence finds exact Polish substitutes and a 24/7 field-service burden inconsistent with the founder's part-time launch constraints.
title: Vendor-Neutral EV Charger Reliability Operations
uncertainties: Addressable count of 20-500-connector Polish and CEE fleets after excluding mobility-only entities, single-site operators, large incumbents, and assets already covered by comprehensive contracts.
Separate annual budget and economic buyer for reliability operations.
Backend, remote-command, log, firmware, payment-data, warranty, and repair rights by fleet and manufacturer.
Polish mixed-brand fault mix, incident rate, remote-close rate, one-visit-close rate, repeat-fault rate, and false-public-status rate.
Technician density, on-call premiums, travel time, parts lead time, UDT delay, and field contribution margin.
Commercial reuse and outreach rights for EIPA-derived fleet and outage reports and contractual rights for non-public operational data.
Paid pilot conversion, CAC, sales cycle, onboarding cost, retention, and service-credit exposure.
Whether the founder can validate under a business-hours SLA when competitors promise 24/7 support.
